sections.html:
Simsbury sits at the northern end of the Farmington Valley in Hartford County, with 24,517 residents at the 2020 census. The Farmington River runs through it, and Talcott Mountain flanks the east side along with Talcott Mountain State Park, Penwood State Park and the Tariffville Gorge. Houses near the river, the ridge and the parks attract their own kind of buyer.

Housing is a patchwork. The population was 4,822 in 1950 and 17,475 by 1970, so a big share of homes are from the postwar boom, set next to much older houses in the historic districts. Condition varies a lot from one street to the next, and that gap is what most sellers have to decide how to handle.

A National Register listing does not by itself create local rules. Whether your own property has local restrictions is a question for the town, and it is worth asking before you plan exterior work or promise a buyer anything.

The villages are Simsbury Center, Tariffville, Weatogue and West Simsbury. In the center, Hopmeadow Street has a run of old public and commercial buildings, including the Phelps Tavern Museum and Homestead at 800 Hopmeadow Street, a 1771 house.

Simsbury Town Hall and the police station share the former Horace Belden School at 933 Hopmeadow Street. It is a sensible first stop for questions about permits, assessments or land records. Call ahead to confirm hours and which office handles your question.

Buyers with children will ask which elementary school serves a house. Simsbury Public Schools has Central, Latimer Lane, Squadron Line, Tariffville and Tootin' Hills, plus Henry James Memorial School for grades 7 and 8 and Simsbury High School. Find the attendance zone for your street and put it in writing.

sections.h2: Work, commuting and moving on short notice
sections.html:
The Board of Education is the town's top employer, and Ensign-Bickford, Chubb and The Hartford are among the companies with a presence here. Many residents commute around greater Hartford, so a job change in insurance or a related field is a common reason for a move.

When a new job starts before the old house is sold, a cash sale can keep you from paying two housing costs. A traditional listing can bring more if you have months to wait and money for repairs, so weigh both with real numbers.

Simsbury gets about 46 inches of precipitation a year, with temperatures that have dropped as low as minus 26. Roofs, heating systems and pipes take the beating. Replace or at least document anything near the end of its life, and keep a vacant house heated.

If your house is near the Farmington River, check its flood zone status with the town before you list, because lenders look at it. Ask for the local flood maps rather than guessing either way.

sections.h2: Foundation problems and the pyrrhotite exemption
sections.html:
Connecticut has a specific conveyance tax exemption for a principal residence with a deteriorating concrete foundation caused by pyrrhotite, as determined by a professional engineer. It applies only to the first transfer after the written evaluation, and a copy of the engineer's report has to be attached to the return.

If you suspect foundation trouble, such as cracking in the concrete walls, hire an engineer before you do anything else. The report decides whether the exemption is available, and it also tells any buyer, cash or otherwise, what they are looking at.

sections.h2: Recording the deed and the state tax
sections.html:
The seller files Connecticut Form OP-236 with the Simsbury town clerk when the deed is recorded. Tax is due once the price reaches two thousand dollars, unless an exemption applies. The town code on the form is 128.

  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on a principal residence is exempt.
  • Estates and trusts that sell attach Schedule A.

Rates change, so ask your closing attorney for current numbers. For a tax bill, contact the Simsbury assessor and tax collector.

The simplest way to compare your choices is to price each one honestly. For a listing, estimate the sale price, subtract repairs, commissions and the months of carrying costs. For an as-is cash offer, there is nothing to subtract but the closing costs and any payoffs. Then look at which gives you the better result and the better timeline.

  1. Gather the deed, mortgage statement and latest tax bill.
  2. Get a contractor's estimate if repairs are on the table.
  3. If there is an estate or a divorce, confirm who has legal authority to sell before anything else.
  4. Choose a closing attorney early, since the title search and the OP-236 both go through that office.

At closing, bring photo ID, keys and any garage openers. Payoffs come out of the proceeds and the rest is yours.

Past-due property taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at the closing table. They do not block a sale, but they do cut into what you walk away with, and interest keeps building until they are settled. Call the tax collector for a payoff figure, and ask whether anything else, like a sewer charge, is open against the parcel.

Give the closing attorney that figure at the start. A title search will turn up any lien anyway, and it is far better to hear about a surprise from your own paperwork than from the buyer's side in the last week.

Once you accept an offer, the order is predictable. The buyer opens title, and the attorney checks the deed history for liens, missing signatures or old mortgages that were never released. Any problem found has to be cleared before the deed can pass. You and the attorney then settle the closing statement, which lists every payoff and charge and shows your net.

With a cash buyer, the period between acceptance and closing is mostly this title work, so it is short if the paperwork is clean and longer if there is an estate to settle or an old lien to remove. Tell the buyer about anything unusual in the house early, including a past foundation concern, and put the agreed terms in writing.

A cash offer lets you sell the house as it stands, and you can decline it. There is no lender appraisal and no repair list after an inspection, so the date is set by the title work and by you. The tradeoff is that the price reflects the work the buyer will take on.

If you want a number for a Simsbury house, call or text us with the address and we will give you a straight answer.

faqs.q: How many people live in Simsbury?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 24,517 residents in a town of about 34.3 square miles.
In the former Horace Belden School at 933 Hopmeadow Street, which also houses the police station. Call ahead to confirm hours and which office handles your question.

faqs.q: Is there a tax break for a pyrrhotite foundation when selling?
faqs.a: Yes. Connecticut exempts the first transfer of a principal residence with a deteriorating concrete foundation, as determined by a professional engineer, from the state conveyance tax. The engineer's report is attached to the return.

faqs.q: Does a National Register listing limit what I can do to my house?
faqs.a: Not by itself. Ask the town whether your property has local restrictions before planning exterior work.

faqs.q: What if the house is an estate sale?
faqs.a: Estates and trusts that sell attach Schedule A to the conveyance tax return. Confirm who has legal authority to sign before you list or accept an offer.
